errors.context: A school wants 20 different pupils from a complete register.
lines: Number every eligible pupil from 1 to 400.
Use a random-number generator set to 1–400.
Keep the first 20 numbers produced, even when a number appears twice.

repairs.text: Keep going until 20 distinct valid numbers have been obtained; ignore repeats.
Replace the generator with a regular interval of 20.
Keep the repeats, but ask those pupils twice.

errors.explanation: Repeated numbers would select the same sampling unit more than once. For a simple random sample without replacement, discard repeats and continue until 20 different pupils have been chosen.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Keeping repeats guarantees 20 distinct pupils because there were 20 draws.
Twenty draws may refer to fewer than 20 different pupils.
A repeated number makes every previously selected pupil ineligible for the study.

impact.explanation: For sampling without replacement, count distinct valid labels, not generator outputs. Repeated labels must be ignored until 20 different pupils are selected.

errors.context: An inspector selects 20 items from a numbered list of 200.
lines: Calculate the interval as 200 ÷ 20 = 10.
Start at item 1 without any random choice.
Take every tenth item until 20 are selected.

repairs.text: Make the interval 20 instead.
Choose a random start from positions 1 to 10, then every tenth item.
Use the first ten items only.

errors.explanation: Systematic sampling needs a random starting position within the first interval (for this exact integer interval). Always starting at 1 makes the choice of start non-random.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Using an interval of ten will always select fewer than 20 items from 200.
Choosing an interval of ten guarantees that each individual item is sampled.
Only one of the ten possible starting positions is used, so many items cannot be selected.

impact.explanation: With k = 10, randomly choose the start from 1 to 10. Fixing it at 1 makes the selection pattern predetermined.

errors.context: A school has separate year-group registers and needs proportional representation.
lines: Divide pupils into non-overlapping year groups.
Calculate the required number from each year group.
Take the first names alphabetically from each group until the target is reached.

repairs.text: Replace the year groups with a single volunteer queue.
Select the specified number randomly within each group, without repeats.
Keep the alphabetical order because the sample sizes are proportional.

errors.explanation: Proportional group numbers alone do not make a sample stratified random: the units within each stratum must be chosen randomly.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Within each year group, surname order determines who is chosen rather than random selection.
The calculation of the number required from each year group becomes impossible.
Alphabetical selection gives all eligible pupils equal probability within each year group.

impact.explanation: Correct proportional group numbers do not fix non-random selection within each stratum.

errors.context: Interviewers have targets of 30 commuters and 20 non-commuters.
lines: Set a numerical target for each group.
Recruit eligible people encountered until each target is filled.
Because the group sizes are fixed, the individuals must have been chosen randomly.

repairs.text: Quota sampling uses non-random selection within groups; targets do not imply random selection.
Interview everyone, so that the investigation becomes a census.
Remove the group targets and only sample every tenth person.

errors.explanation: A quota sets targets but typically fills them by approaching available respondents. Proportional quotas are not the same as random selection within strata.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Meeting a quota is sufficient to make every individual equally likely to be chosen.
The quotas fix group totals but do not make the choice of individuals random.
The two quotas must be equal for this method to count as quota sampling.

impact.explanation: Quota sampling fills preset categories by non-random recruitment; it is not automatically stratified random sampling.

errors.context: A calculator is explicitly programmed to generate integers only from 1 to 150.
lines: Number the 150 eligible people from 1 to 150.
Generate random integers in the inclusive range 1–150.
Reject any number outside 1–150 because this restricted generator regularly produces them.

repairs.text: Use a random starting position and take every tenth person.
Retain all repeats until the sample size is reached.
Discard repeats, but out-of-range rejection is unnecessary with a generator restricted to 1–150.

errors.explanation: A generator constrained to 1–150 cannot produce out-of-range numbers. Ignore repeats; exclude invalid numbers only when the random source can actually produce them.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Restricting the random integers to 1–150 makes repeated values impossible.
The valid range makes it unnecessary to give each eligible person a unique label.
The claimed out-of-range values cannot occur with this restricted generator.

impact.explanation: Range restrictions prevent out-of-range outputs, not repeated outputs. Repeats still need to be ignored when selecting distinct units.

errors.context: A researcher wants a random sample of every club member, including new members.
lines: Obtain last term's register, which excludes the new members.
Assign a unique number to everyone on that old register.
Generate distinct random numbers and contact those people.

repairs.text: Include the new members in a complete up-to-date sampling frame before numbering.
Choose every fifth name in the old register.
Describe the old register as representative because random numbers are used.

errors.explanation: Random selection from an incomplete frame cannot include units that are missing from it. A complete eligible-population frame is essential.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: New club members have zero chance of selection because they are missing from the frame.
Using random numbers makes every new member equally likely to be chosen anyway.
An older list makes the random numbers themselves non-uniform.

impact.explanation: Uniform selection within a frame cannot repair omissions from the frame; coverage of the target population is incomplete.

errors.context: A school has 300 Year 12 and 200 Year 13 pupils. A proportional sample of 50 is wanted.
lines: Separate the two year groups.
Allocate 25 places to Year 12 and 25 to Year 13 because there are two strata.
Randomly select the allocated number from each year-group register.

repairs.text: Take 50 from each year group.
Allocate 30 to Year 12 and 20 to Year 13, then sample randomly within each.
Use 25 each but label it proportional because there are two groups.

errors.explanation: Proportional allocation is 50×300/500=30 and 50×200/500=20. Equal allocation is not proportional when the group sizes differ.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Year 12 is overrepresented: its share in the sample is larger than 60%.
Year 13 is overrepresented: its sample share is 50%, but its population share is 40%.
Equal numbers from each year group are proportional because there are two groups.

impact.explanation: The sample should contain 30 Year 12 and 20 Year 13 pupils, reflecting the 60%/40% population split.

errors.context: A survey team plans a sample from a complete population list.
lines: Number the population and select distinct numbers randomly.
Apply the resulting sample to the survey.
A simple random sample is guaranteed to be representative because it is random.

repairs.text: Random sampling removes every possible bias, so the claim is correct.
A census never has response errors, unlike sampling.
Random selection gives a probability design but does not guarantee a representative realised sample.

errors.explanation: Random selection can produce an unbalanced sample by chance, and nonresponse can introduce bias. Representativeness is not guaranteed.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Random selection forces every subgroup to be included in its exact population proportion.
An unbalanced result proves that the original random-number generator was unfair.
A valid random sample may still underrepresent some subgroups by chance.

impact.explanation: Random sampling gives an appropriate probability mechanism, not a guarantee about the composition of the realised sample.

errors.context: A factory's packing list follows a repeating colour sequence every 10 items.
lines: Order the full list and choose an interval of 10.
Use a random start within the first ten positions.
The random start ensures the repeating list order cannot cause a distorted sample.

repairs.text: A random start does not eliminate a periodicity risk; investigate or change the ordering/design.
Always start at item 1 to prevent periodicity.
Choose a quota sample but call it systematic.

errors.explanation: When the sampling interval matches a periodic pattern, one start may select only one phase of the pattern. Check for periodic ordering.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: All selected items may belong to the same phase of the repeating ten-item sequence.
A random start always includes a balanced selection of every phase of the sequence.
Selecting every tenth item prevents any of the listed colours from being sampled.

impact.explanation: A random start alone cannot remove the periodicity risk when a sampling interval matches a repeated list pattern.

errors.context: A travel survey sets 40 morning and 60 afternoon respondent targets.
lines: Decide and communicate the two quotas.
Recruit the first eligible volunteers available in each period.
Classify the method as stratified random because it has two groups.

repairs.text: The use of a survey makes the method a census.
It is quota sampling: there is no random selection of individuals within each group.
It is simple random because group targets were set.

errors.explanation: Having groups is insufficient to make a design stratified random. Without random selection within the groups, this is quota sampling.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Any use of two groups makes the selection random within each group.
The chosen individuals are recruited non-randomly, even though the quotas are filled.
Using volunteers means group totals cannot be specified in advance.

impact.explanation: Group targets are not the distinguishing feature of stratified random sampling; random selection within groups is.

errors.context: A researcher needs 40 from an ordered register of 197.
lines: The planned ratio N/n is 197/40 = 4.925.
Choose a random start of 1 from the first five positions, then take every fifth entry; this particular start gives 40 entries.
Claim that rounding N/n to the nearest integer is the universal systematic rule and always returns the requested n.

repairs.text: Start at 1 and keep the rounded rule, which always works.
A non-integer ratio needs a deliberately specified suitable systematic pattern and count check; no universal rounding rule exists.
Ignore all people after the first 40 entries.

errors.explanation: Starting at 1 gives 40 entries, but other possible starts can give only 39. Rounding the interval is not a universal rule for a non-integer N/n; check how the proposed scheme achieves the required number.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Every start from 1 to 5 gives exactly 40 selected positions from 197.
A non-integer population-to-sample ratio prevents any systematic sample being taken.
With every fifth entry, some starting positions select only 39, not the requested 40.

impact.explanation: For 197 entries and every fifth selection, starts 1 or 2 give 40; starts 3, 4 or 5 give 39. The method must specify and check how to obtain 40.

errors.context: A school wants views from all students but asks only students in the canteen at 12:30.
lines: Define the target population as all students.
Ask those who are available at the canteen at 12:30.
Conclude that this gives an unbiased picture of all students because it is easy to carry out.

repairs.text: Treat the canteen group as an opportunity sample with possible time/location selection bias; broaden recruitment.
Describe all pupils at school as having been observed.
Choose every fifth canteen visitor and claim all students are equally likely.

errors.explanation: Being available at a particular place and time may correlate with the behaviour being studied and exclude groups. Ease is not representativeness.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Students absent from the canteen at that time have no opportunity to be selected.
Everyone in the school has an equal chance because the canteen is on campus.
An opportunity sample is a census as long as the interviewer asks everyone nearby.

impact.explanation: Selection is restricted to one place and time. Students elsewhere may differ from canteen users, creating possible coverage bias.

errors.context: A survey aims for 55 out of 550, with strata sizes 205, 190 and 155.
lines: Allocate approximately 20.5, 19 and 15.5 places to the three strata.
Allocate 21, 19 and 15 whole-number places, totalling 55.
Randomly take 21, 19 and 16 people from the strata and report a sample size of 55.

repairs.text: Take the first 55 names regardless of strata.
Round all three down and sample only 54 people.
Draw the allocated 21, 19 and 15 people randomly within the respective strata, totalling 55.

errors.explanation: Although the intended allocation 21 + 19 + 15 = 55 is defensible, the proposed draw 21 + 19 + 16 = 56. The final draw must match whole-number allocations summing to 55.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: The specified selection totals only 54, so the sample is too small.
The specified selection totals 56, exceeding the intended sample size of 55.
Proportional stratified samples must have equal numbers drawn from every stratum.

impact.explanation: 21 + 19 + 16 = 56. A defensible whole-number allocation such as 21, 19, 15 totals 55; the actual draw must use those totals.

errors.context: A researcher uses an unrestricted random-digit table for numbers 001–180.
lines: Create a full numbered frame 001 to 180.
Read three-digit groups from the random-digit table.
Retain values such as 000 and 924 as valid selections, as long as they have not appeared before.

repairs.text: Keep all values if no duplicate appears.
Reject values outside 001–180 and any repeats; continue until enough distinct units are chosen.
Replace the sampling frame with only the first 100 units.

errors.explanation: Unlike a constrained 1–180 generator, a random-digit table can produce invalid values. Reject out-of-range values and repeats.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Three-digit random tables are incapable of producing 000.
A random table makes repeated labels acceptable in a sample without replacement.
000 and 924 do not identify anybody in the numbered population 001–180.

impact.explanation: Reject groups outside 001–180 as well as repeats when reading unrestricted random digits, and keep sampling until enough distinct valid labels appear.

errors.context: An investigation compares the breakfast habits of all town residents.
lines: Interview the first 30 willing shoppers at one supermarket on Monday morning.
Record their responses accurately.
Describe the survey as covering the target population equally because the sample is convenient.

repairs.text: Convenience alone makes it representative if n=30.
Treat the result as an opportunity sample with likely coverage and nonresponse limitations; sample at other times/places or use a suitable frame.
Claim all town residents are equally likely to visit that supermarket at that time.

errors.explanation: The recruited people are only those available and willing at one place and time, not a random cross-section of all town residents.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Residents who do not shop there at that time may be excluded, making representation uncertain.
Recording accurate responses guarantees that the selection of shoppers was random.
A sample of 30 guarantees that the town's demographic groups are represented.

impact.explanation: Recording responses accurately does not correct a convenience-based sampling frame. Other times, sites or probability methods could broaden coverage.

errors.context: A club has 120 numbered members and needs a systematic sample of 20.
lines: Use the complete list of 120 numbered members.
Calculate the fixed selection interval as 120 ÷ 20 = 5.
Choose a random start within the first interval, then continue using that interval.

repairs.text: Use interval 6 because 120 ÷ 20 = 6, then randomly choose a start from positions 1–6.
Use interval 20, since that is the number of members needed.
Avoid the random start and simply choose the first member.

errors.explanation: For an exact integer interval, k = N/n = 120/20 = 6. An interval of five would produce too many selections if the list were traversed fully.

impact.question: What happens if the chosen interval stays at five?

options.text: The first 20 members are always chosen, regardless of the starting point.
Selecting every fifth member across 120 positions would give 24 members, not the required 20.
The selection automatically becomes quota sampling because the interval is too small.

impact.explanation: The interval determines how many positions are visited; the random start alone cannot correct the wrong ratio.

errors.context: A college has 180 Year 12 pupils and 60 Year 13 pupils and wants a proportional random sample of 40.
lines: Divide the pupils into their separate year-group registers.
Allocate 20 selections to each year group because there are two groups.
Randomly choose the allocated number of distinct pupils within each register.

repairs.text: Allocate all 40 places to Year 12 because it is the larger group.
Allocate 30 pupils to Year 12 and 10 to Year 13, matching the 180:60 population ratio.
Keep equal allocations and describe the result as a proportional design.

errors.explanation: Proportional stratification requires 40×180/240=30 from Year 12 and 40×60/240=10 from Year 13, not equal numbers.

impact.question: What is the consequence of keeping 20 from each group?

options.text: The sample would necessarily contain more than 40 pupils.
Every possible group of 40 pupils would still be equally likely.
Year 13 would form 50% of the sample despite being only 25% of the population.

impact.explanation: Equal subgroup counts are not proportional when the population groups have different sizes.

errors.context: A sports centre wants 12 adult and 8 teenage volunteers for a survey using quota sampling.
lines: Set an adult target of 12 and a teenage target of 8.
Approach willing eligible visitors and record the group for each response.
Keep recruiting adults even after 12 adult responses have been obtained, provided the total is below 20.

repairs.text: Draw every name randomly from a complete membership register instead.
Remove the two subgroup targets and take any 20 available visitors.
Stop recruiting from a group as soon as its target is reached; continue only with unfilled groups.

errors.explanation: Quota sampling uses fixed subgroup counts. Taking extra adults when their quota is full prevents the intended 12:8 allocation.

impact.question: What could the incorrect stopping rule do?

options.text: The sample could exceed the adult quota and fail to contain eight teenagers.
It makes the procedure a census of all visitors.
It guarantees random selection within each age group.

impact.explanation: A correct total of 20 is insufficient when the stated quotas must also be met.

errors.context: A library volunteer surveys 25 pupils who are available in the library at lunchtime.
lines: Approach pupils who happen to be in the library at lunchtime.
Record each willing pupil's response until 25 have taken part.
Tell the headteacher that every pupil in the school had an equal chance of selection.

repairs.text: Describe it as an opportunity sample and explain that pupils absent from the library were not available.
Call the sample stratified because pupils may belong to different year groups.
Treat 25 responses as a census of the whole school.

errors.explanation: A convenient, location-based sample has unequal inclusion opportunities: pupils who do not attend the library at that time cannot be selected.

impact.question: What is the main risk in generalising the responses?

options.text: Every pupil was selected with a known probability of 25 divided by the school size.
Library users could have different habits from pupils who do not visit at lunchtime.
The data necessarily contain no measurement or recording errors.

impact.explanation: Convenience sampling may introduce coverage and selection bias, even when responses are accurately recorded.

errors.context: A student seeks quick opinions about a canteen change by asking whoever is near the entrance after lunch.
lines: Approach eligible volunteers encountered at the canteen entrance.
Stop after the planned 20 responses without setting subgroup targets.
Label the method simple random sampling because the student did not choose the order of people arriving.

repairs.text: Label it stratified because some respondents are different ages.
Label the method opportunity sampling because recruitment depends on who is available, not an impartial random draw.
Keep the simple random label because any order of arrival is automatically random.

errors.explanation: An unplanned arrival order does not make every sample of 20 equally likely. No chance-based selection procedure has been used.

impact.question: Why might the resulting sample be unrepresentative?

options.text: A sample size of 20 guarantees the same preferences as the population.
Arrival order ensures every possible group of 20 pupils is equally probable.
Pupils absent from the canteen or passing at a different time have little or no chance of inclusion.

impact.explanation: Convenient access is the selection rule; the absence of deliberate choice is not equivalent to simple random sampling.

errors.context: An inspection list repeats a cycle of three machine types, and a researcher wants every third record.
lines: Keep the production-order list, which repeats types A, B and C.
Choose a random starting record among the first three.
Assume the random start guarantees all three machine types will be represented in the sample.

repairs.text: Drop the random start but keep every third record because that removes bias.
Increase the number selected without examining the repeating pattern.
Check the ordering first: every third record may sample only one machine type; change the frame/order or design if coverage matters.

errors.explanation: A period-three ordering combined with an interval of three locks each sample into one of the repeating categories, whatever the random start.

impact.question: What might an entire sample contain?

options.text: All selected records might belong to one machine type, misleading an investigation about all types.
Each machine type must appear exactly one-third of the time.
Random starts remove the effect of all periodic patterns in the ordered list.

impact.explanation: A random starting position does not eliminate periodicity when the interval matches the list's cycle.

errors.context: An employer wants a proportionate random sample from two distinct department registers.
lines: Calculate the sample allocation for each department from its population share.
Take the first available employees in each department until those totals are met.
Combine the resulting responses and call them a stratified random sample.

repairs.text: Randomly select the required distinct employee IDs within each department rather than taking those first available.
Keep the convenient selection because proportions alone make the sample random.
Replace departmental allocation with a fixed gap through one undivided employee list.

errors.explanation: The stated allocation is proportional, but selecting employees for convenience within departments is not stratified random sampling.

impact.question: Which problem arises from recruiting the first available workers?

options.text: The procedure guarantees every employee equal inclusion probability.
Availability within departments may be associated with shifts or roles, creating selection bias.
Departments cannot be included if a random selection is used.

impact.explanation: Random selection must occur separately within each stratum, not just in how many places each receives.

errors.context: Surveyors must recruit 20 commuters by bus and 20 by car outside a station.
lines: Use separate targets of 20 bus commuters and 20 car commuters.
Approach available, willing commuters in each category until both totals are filled.
State that setting equal quotas has removed all possible selection and nonresponse bias.

repairs.text: Treat the sample as a census because it includes both commuter groups.
Explain that convenience recruitment and refusals can still bias the sample even if the quotas are filled.
Assume everyone approached has the same likelihood of response.

errors.explanation: Quota controls the specified category totals, not the characteristics or response propensity of people recruited within them.

impact.question: What may remain hidden despite the 20:20 totals?

options.text: Two quotas ensure that all journeys are recorded.
A numerical target implies that every individual in both groups was selected randomly.
Unwilling or absent commuters may systematically differ from willing respondents inside each category.

impact.explanation: Representing two selected category counts does not establish unbiased selection or response.

errors.context: A survey claims to describe all students but interviews those waiting outside a gym after school.
lines: Recruit the first 30 willing pupils outside the gym after clubs end.
Record the pupils' answers accurately.
Use the resulting percentages as exact estimates of the entire school's views without qualification.

repairs.text: Claim accurate data entry proves the gym sample is random.
Count 30 responses as a census if everyone near the gym responded.
Explain that this convenient time and place may favour club members and report the coverage limitation.

errors.explanation: The sample may omit students who do not attend clubs or wait near the gym, so unrestricted population claims are unjustified.

impact.question: Who may be systematically underrepresented?

options.text: Pupils who leave immediately or do not attend after-school activities.
All school pupils have the same probability of being outside the gym.
The selection mechanism cannot influence survey results if responses are recorded carefully.

impact.explanation: An accurate response from a biased selection is still not an unbiased sample of the school.

errors.context: A town survey uses volunteers visiting a public market on a weekday morning.
lines: Interview available eligible market visitors during the morning.
Record how many people decline to participate.
Assume the results apply equally to people who work weekday mornings and never visit the market.

repairs.text: Qualify conclusions to the accessible group and sample at additional times/locations or use a resident frame.
Ignore refusals because the willing volunteers supply enough answers.
Call it systematic sampling because interviews happen in sequence.

errors.explanation: The sampling location and time exclude many residents, and willingness to respond may further distort results.

impact.question: What might the timing do to the estimate?

options.text: A market automatically contains every subgroup in the town.
Residents working at that time may be missed, leaving an overrepresentation of available visitors.
Recording refusals makes unavailable residents part of the sampled frame.

impact.explanation: Monitoring nonresponse is useful, but it cannot fix residents who never had a chance to be approached.

errors.context: An online university has 1,000 eligible students, but an extract lists only 870 with current email addresses.
lines: Use the 870-address extract as the only list of selectable students.
Generate distinct random numbers from 1 to 870 to invite 80 students.
Claim that every possible group of 80 from all 1,000 students has the same selection probability.

repairs.text: Keep the claim because 80 random numbers eliminate every source of bias.
Acknowledge incomplete coverage and seek a complete eligible-student frame before claiming a simple random sample of all 1,000.
Relabel the extract a census so the missing 130 do not matter.

errors.explanation: Random selection from an incomplete frame cannot give omitted students a positive inclusion probability.

impact.question: What is the probability that one of the 130 omitted students is selected?

options.text: Exactly 80/1,000, because that is the target sample fraction.
The same as every student with a recorded email address.
Zero, even though they belong to the defined population of 1,000.

impact.explanation: A fair generator only selects from labels it can produce; missing units are excluded before the draw.

errors.context: An analyst needs 40 of 197 sequential records and plans an interval of five.
lines: Choose a random start anywhere from positions 1 to 5.
Select that record and every fifth record until exactly 40 have been chosen.
Use only positions that lie between 1 and 197.

repairs.text: Allow starts 1–5 and discard any selected positions above 197; exactly 40 are still guaranteed.
Always start at position 5, since 197 divided by 40 is almost 5.
For this interval and size, restrict the random start to 1 or 2 so the 40th position stays at most 197.

errors.explanation: The 40th selected position is start+39×5=start+195. It is at most 197 only for start≤2; starts 3,4,5 would leave the frame.

impact.question: What happens with a random start of five?

options.text: The 40th position is 200, outside the 197-record frame, so the proposed procedure cannot give 40 valid positions.
The 40th position is 195 and always remains within the frame.
Every possible group of 40 records becomes equally likely after rounding.

impact.explanation: A non-integer N/n calls for a defensible interval/start rule; it has no universal mandatory rounding procedure.

errors.context: A researcher randomly selects proportional numbers from two student-year registers, but some selected pupils do not reply.
lines: Randomly draw the prescribed distinct pupils from each stratum.
For each pupil who refuses, substitute a willing friend from the same year group.
Report the final responses as a fully random stratified sample with no nonresponse concern.

repairs.text: Follow up selected nonrespondents where appropriate, record stratum-specific response rates, and explain any remaining nonresponse risk.
Replace each nonrespondent with the nearest available pupil and omit the replacement rule.
Claim that a matching year-group label restores the original random selection.

errors.explanation: Substituting convenience-based friends changes the selection probabilities and risks introducing bias, despite preserving nominal year totals.

impact.question: What can replacing nonrespondents with friends distort?

options.text: It guarantees every original sampled pupil's response has been recorded.
Respondents' friendship networks and willingness to participate may affect the final sample within each stratum.
Group proportions alone ensure all individual selection probabilities remain unaffected.

impact.explanation: The realised responding sample is not automatically random just because its planned allocation was proportional.

errors.context: A town study fills 60 urban and 40 rural survey places through available volunteers.
lines: Set the 60:40 urban/rural quotas from the population proportions.
Recruit willing respondents until both specified totals are met.
Claim that matching one population characteristic proves the final results are representative of every demographic and outcome.

repairs.text: Call the design stratified random because it uses correct population proportions.
State that quota controls only the chosen grouping and that within-group convenience selection can still create bias.
Treat the collected sample as a census of urban and rural residents.

errors.explanation: Population-matching quotas do not automatically balance age, income, participation or the outcome being investigated.

impact.question: Which limitation survives matching the urban/rural quotas?

options.text: Every eligible resident had equal probability of selection.
Matching one margin forces all other sample characteristics to match the population.
Differences between volunteers and non-volunteers within each area can distort estimates.

impact.explanation: Quota sampling controls chosen targets but does not provide random within-quota selection.

errors.context: A health survey recruits volunteers aged 18–30 and 30–45 using quotas of 25 in each age bracket.
lines: Define one bracket as 18–30 inclusive and the other as 30–45 inclusive.
Keep a running count against the two 25-person targets.
Ask available eligible volunteers until both counters show 25.

repairs.text: Count 30-year-olds twice to satisfy both quotas more efficiently.
Remove all age-group counts so the study becomes a proportional quota sample.
Define non-overlapping age categories, for example 18–29 and 30–45 for whole ages, before recruitment.

errors.explanation: Age 30 belongs to both stated brackets, so the categories are not mutually exclusive and the quota membership is ambiguous.

impact.question: What could happen if 30-year-olds are counted in both categories?

options.text: A single respondent could fill two nominal places, preventing the intended two-group composition.
Double counting creates a simple random sample.
Overlapping brackets ensure exactly 50 distinct respondents have been recruited.

impact.explanation: Quotas require clear, non-overlapping classification rules when separate group totals are intended.
